fields.title: How Permissions Break
fields.keyTakeaway: Permissions accumulate if they are not revoked, so you need a default lifespan, last use display, and regular review — including for your own employees' access.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: The permissions model is designed correctly. Where do extra access rights still come from?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Permissions have a habit of accumulating: they are granted and not revoked. After two years a typical employee has access to what was needed for three previous tasks. Each extra access increases the damage during a compromise.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Granted and forgotten.** Access for a task remained forever. Fixed by default temporary access.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Internal transfer.** A person changed roles, old permissions remained. Fixed by review upon role change and regular audits.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **[[privilege-escalation|Privilege escalation]] through combination.** Each permission separately is harmless, together they grant more. Classics: permission to change settings plus permission to view the log allows disabling logging and acting unnoticed.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **Service accounts.** Accounts for integrations are often created with wide permissions "so that it definitely works" and live for years.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: What the product does about this:
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: *Access review.* Once a quarter the client administrator confirms the list. A mechanism in the interface, not an email. *Last use display.* A permission that hasn't been used in half a year is visible and removed. *Default expiration.* Extended permissions are granted for a period, renewed explicitly.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: Separately — **our own access to client data.** This is the same question, and corporate questionnaires ask it. The answer "employees have access on a need-to-know basis with logging and for a duration" is substantially better than "employees have access".
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Access review in the partner account: once a quarter the administrator is shown a list of employees with the last login date and a prompt to confirm or disable. The first review at three large chains disabled 34% of accounts.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: Service accounts for integrations: used to have full permissions, became scope "orders only, read-only, own store only". One integrator complained it stopped working — it turned out they were reading data they didn't need.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Our access: permanent support access replaced by temporary. In questionnaires this is an item now passed with log attachments.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: Permission combination: discovered that a store manager could disable logging in their store. Removed — logging cannot be disabled by anyone on the client side.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Too frequent reviews are perceived as bureaucracy and passed through without looking. A quarter is a reasonable interval; more frequent makes sense only for critical permissions.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Permissions accumulate if they are not revoked, so you need a default lifespan, last use display, and regular review — including for your own employees' access.
